# Task: Implement RecJPQPrune as a native Faiss index

## 1. Objective

Implement RecJPQPrune as a new Faiss index class, providing exact top-K retrieval over a collection of RecJPQ-compressed item embeddings.

The implementation must follow the algorithm described in:

Petrov et al., "Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings", SIGIR 2025.

Paper:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.00560

Reference implementation:
https://github.com/asash/recjpq_dp_pruning/blob/main/pruned_score_batch.py

The implementation should be written in C++ and integrated into the existing Faiss architecture.

The goal is to expose RecJPQPrune through the standard Faiss search interface, allowing it to be used similarly to other Faiss indexes.

Do not implement a conventional IVF index. RecJPQPrune has a different inverted-index structure and retrieval algorithm.

## 2. Faiss integration

Create a new class:

    faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune

The class should derive from:

    faiss::Index

Do not derive from IndexFlatCodes or IndexIVF.

The index represents a collection of RecJPQ-compressed item embeddings.

It must implement the relevant Faiss Index interface:

- add / add_with_ids, as appropriate for the chosen construction API (you may assume that the Index is built from an existing IndexPQ)
- search
- reset
- reconstruct, if practical
- ntotal
- is_trained
- metric_type

Use METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT as the primary metric.

The query is a dense embedding vector, and retrieval returns the K items with the highest inner-product scores.

The class should follow the coding conventions, API conventions, error handling and build-system integration of the existing Faiss codebase.

Inspect the Faiss version in the repository before implementing the interface. Do not assume signatures from another Faiss version.

## 3. Data model

RecJPQ represents each item using M sub-item IDs.

Define:

- N: number of indexed items
- M: number of subquantizer splits
- B: number of sub-item IDs per split
- d: full embedding dimensionality
- ds = d / M: dimensionality of each split
- K: requested number of nearest items

Each item i is represented by:

    item_codes[i][m] ∈ [0, B)

The full item embedding is constructed by concatenating the corresponding sub-item embeddings.

Store the following information:

### 3.1 Item codes

A matrix of dimensions:

    N × M

Use uint8_t when B <= 256.

The implementation should validate the supported code range and document any restrictions on B.

The item code matrix should be stored contiguously in row-major order.

### 3.2 Sub-item embedding tables

Store the RecJPQ codebooks:

    codebooks[M][B][ds]

Each split has B sub-item embeddings, each with dimensionality ds.

The original RecJPQ item embedding is:

    w_i = concat(
        codebooks[0][item_codes[i][0]],
        ...
        codebooks[M-1][item_codes[i][M-1]]
    )

### 3.3 External document IDs

Support arbitrary int64 Faiss IDs.

Maintain a mapping between internal contiguous item positions and external IDs.

The inverted lists should store internal item positions for efficient candidate scoring.

The final search results must return external IDs.

The internal position is in [0, N), while the external ID is an arbitrary faiss::idx_t.

Do not assume that external IDs are contiguous or equal to internal positions.

## 4. Inverted-index implementation

Implement a dedicated CSR-based inverted index.

Suggested class:

    RecJPQInvertedLists

The index contains M × B posting lists.

The posting-list identifier is:

    list_id = split * B + sub_item_id

Each posting list contains the internal positions of all items whose code at that split equals the corresponding sub-item ID.

Use CSR-style storage:

    std::vector<size_t> offsets;
    std::vector<faiss::idx_t> item_ids;

A posting list is represented by:

    begin = offsets[list_id]
    end   = offsets[list_id + 1]

    items = item_ids[begin:end]

Requirements:

- Two-pass construction.
- First pass counts items per posting list.
- Prefix sum constructs offsets.
- Second pass fills contiguous item-ID storage.
- Posting lists must not contain padding values.
- Support empty posting lists.
- Preserve the internal item positions.
- Provide efficient sequential access to posting-list contents.

Expose methods similar to:

    build(codes, N, M, B)

    list_size(split, sub_item_id)

    get_list(split, sub_item_id)

    get_list_range(split, sub_item_id)

The implementation should not require one heap allocation per posting list.

Do not use the dense, padded representation from the TensorFlow implementation as the primary C++ storage format.

CSR is preferred for memory efficiency and cache locality.

## 5. Query scoring

The input query is a dense vector:

    phi ∈ R^d

Split the query into M subvectors:

    phi = concat(phi_0, ..., phi_(M-1))

For every split m and sub-item ID b, calculate:

    S[m][b] = dot(codebooks[m][b], phi_m)

S is the sub-item score matrix:

    S ∈ R^(M × B)

The score of item i is:

    score(i) = sum(
        S[m][item_codes[i][m]]
        for m in 0 ... M-1
    )

This is exactly the RecJPQ/PQTopK scoring function.

Precompute S once per query.

Candidate scoring must use this lookup table instead of reconstructing the full item embedding or performing a full-dimensional dot product for every candidate.

Use float32 initially.

Support efficient scoring of batches of candidate item positions.

Keep the scoring implementation separate from candidate generation so that it can be optimised independently.

## 6. RecJPQPrune algorithm

Implement Algorithm 1 from Section 4.2 of the paper.

Inputs:

- Query phi
- Codebooks G
- Inverted lists L_1 ... L_M
- Number of results K
- Batch size BS

### 6.1 Initialisation

Calculate the sub-item score matrix S.

For each split m:

1. Sort all B sub-item IDs in descending order of S[m][b].
2. Store the sorted IDs in Q[m].
3. Initialise the current position P[m] = 0.

Define the remaining-score upper bound:

    sigma = sum(
        S[m][Q[m][P[m]]]
        for all m
    )

Initialise:

    theta = -infinity

    R_K = empty top-K result set

### 6.2 Main iteration

While:

    sigma > theta

Perform the following:

1. Identify the split with the highest-scoring unprocessed sub-item:

       m_star = argmax_m S[m][Q[m][P[m]]]

2. Select the next BS sub-item IDs from that split:

       Q[m_star][P[m_star] ... P[m_star] + BS - 1]

   Clamp the batch at B.

3. Retrieve the posting lists for those sub-item IDs:

       candidates = union(
           L[m_star][Q[m_star][j]]
       )

4. Score the candidates using the PQTopK lookup-table scoring function.

5. Merge the scored candidates with the current top-K result set.

6. Deduplicate repeated item IDs.

7. Update the pointer:

       P[m_star] += BS

8. Recalculate the upper bound:

       sigma = sum(
           S[m][Q[m][P[m]]]
           if P[m] < B
           else -infinity
           for all m
       )

9. Update the threshold:

       theta = score of the K-th best item in R_K

Terminate when:

    sigma <= theta

Return R_K.

### 6.3 Correctness requirements

The default implementation must be safe and exact.

The pruning condition must guarantee that no unscored item can enter the final top-K.

Do not use an approximate pruning threshold by default.

In particular:

- ub_inflation must default to 1.0.
- Do not inflate the threshold in safe mode.
- Do not terminate early based on an arbitrary iteration limit.
- Do not silently return fewer than K results when K valid indexed items exist.
- Handle negative scores correctly.
- Handle empty posting lists.
- Handle batch sizes larger than the number of remaining sub-item IDs.

For deterministic tie handling, define and document a consistent tie-breaking policy. If exact top-K ordering must include deterministic ties, do not terminate while an unprocessed item could tie the current K-th score and win under that policy.

If the maximum iteration setting is reached, report that the search was incomplete rather than claiming an exact result.

## 7. Candidate deduplication

An item appears in exactly one posting list per split.

Consequently, the same item can be encountered in multiple iterations and across different splits.

Avoid repeatedly scoring the same item.

Use an efficient visited structure indexed by internal item position.

Recommended approach:

    std::vector<uint32_t> visited;
    uint32_t current_query_generation;

For each query:

    ++current_query_generation

An item is new if:

    visited[item_position] != current_query_generation

When encountering a new item:

    visited[item_position] = current_query_generation

Add it to the candidate batch.

This avoids allocating and clearing an N-sized boolean array for every query.

Handle generation counter overflow safely.

If search is parallelised across queries, visited state must be query-local or thread-local. Never share mutable deduplication state between concurrent searches.

## 8. Top-K maintenance

Implement an efficient top-K structure.

Initially, correctness is more important than micro-optimisation.

A simple implementation may:

- Score each candidate batch.
- Merge the results with the existing top-K.
- Remove duplicate internal item positions.
- Keep the K highest-scoring unique items.

The top-K structure must maintain:

    item_position
    external_id
    score

The threshold theta must always be the score of the current K-th best unique item.

If fewer than K unique candidates have been scored, theta remains negative infinity.

Do not use a merge operation that assumes candidate batches contain unique IDs.

Do not discard candidates based on an incorrect local top-K calculation.

After correctness is established, optimise using a fixed-size min-heap or partial selection.

## 9. Faiss search interface

Implement search using the normal Faiss interface:

    void search(
        idx_t n,
        const float* x,
        idx_t k,
        float* distances,
        idx_t* labels,
        const SearchParameters* params = nullptr
    ) const override;

Check the actual signature for the Faiss version being used.

For each query:

1. Calculate S.
2. Run RecJPQPrune.
3. Return K scores and corresponding external IDs.

Follow Faiss conventions:

- Higher inner-product scores are better.
- Return results in descending score order.
- Fill missing results with -infinity and -1 where appropriate.
- Respect the requested K.
- Support multiple queries in one call.
- Avoid shared mutable state between queries.

The first implementation may process queries sequentially. Later optimise parallelism across queries using OpenMP or the relevant Faiss threading mechanisms.

The implementation must be safe when multiple threads call search concurrently.

## 10. Construction API

Provide a construction API that allows the user to supply:

- M
- B
- d
- Item codes
- Sub-item embedding tables
- Optional external item IDs

One possible API is:

    IndexRecJPQPrune(
        size_t d,
        size_t M,
        size_t B
    );

    void build(
        size_t n,
        const uint8_t* item_codes,
        const float* codebooks,
        const idx_t* ids = nullptr
    );

Alternatively, integrate these arguments into a dedicated constructor or factory method if that better matches Faiss conventions.

Do not require full, uncompressed item embeddings.

The index should be built directly from RecJPQ codes and codebooks.

Ensure that ownership and lifetime of all supplied data are clearly defined.

## 11. Configuration parameters

Provide the following search parameters:

- top_k: supplied through the standard search interface.
- batch_size: number of sub-item IDs processed per iteration (BS).
- max_iterations: optional safety limit; disabled or effectively unlimited in exact mode.
- ub_inflation: default 1.0.
- exact_mode: default true.

Batch size should be configurable independently of index construction.

The safe implementation must preserve exactness for all supported batch sizes.

An optional approximate mode may be implemented later, but must be clearly separated from exact mode.

## 12. Performance requirements

Optimise for large item catalogues (millions of items).

Priorities:

1. Contiguous CSR inverted-list storage.
2. Efficient posting-list traversal.
3. Efficient candidate deduplication.
4. Vectorised PQ lookup-table scoring.
5. Efficient top-K merging.
6. Minimal allocations during search.
7. Query-level parallelism.

Avoid:

- Dense padded inverted lists.
- Per-posting-list heap allocations.
- Reconstructing full item embeddings during candidate scoring.
- Recomputing the sub-item score matrix during each iteration.
- Hash-based deduplication if a direct internal-position lookup is possible.

Reuse per-query scratch buffers where safe.

Do not compromise exactness to improve performance.

## 13. Testing and validation

Create unit tests covering:

### A. Inverted-index correctness

Generate a small synthetic RecJPQ dataset.

Verify that every item occurs in exactly one posting list per split.

Verify that each posting list contains exactly the expected item positions.

Verify arbitrary external IDs are preserved in search results.

### B. Scoring correctness

Compare the lookup-table item score against a direct full-dimensional dot product.

They must agree within a reasonable floating-point tolerance.

### C. Search correctness

Implement an exhaustive PQTopK baseline:

    score(i) = sum_m S[m][item_codes[i][m]]

Sort all N items and select the exact top K.

Compare RecJPQPrune against this baseline.

The returned item IDs and scores must match the exhaustive baseline, subject to the documented tie-breaking policy.

### D. Edge cases

Test:

- K = 1.
- K = N.
- K > N.
- N = 0.
- M = 1.
- B = 1.
- Batch size = 1.
- Batch size > B.
- Empty posting lists.
- Negative scores.
- All scores equal.
- Duplicate external IDs, if supported by the chosen API.
- Arbitrary non-contiguous external IDs.
- Multiple concurrent queries.
- Large catalogues.

### E. Performance benchmarks

Benchmark against exhaustive PQTopK.

Measure:

- Index construction time.
- Index memory consumption.
- Query latency.
- Median latency.
- P95 latency.
- Number of iterations.
- Number of unique items scored.
- Number of posting-list entries traversed.
- Fraction of catalogue scored.

Test several batch sizes, for example:

    BS = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64

Use realistic configurations:

    M = 8
    B = 256
    N = 1,000,000+

Where possible, benchmark with the same data and scoring configuration as the original TensorFlow implementation.

## 14. Reference implementation analysis

Use the authors' pruned_score_batch.py as a reference for practical implementation details.

In particular, examine:

- Sorted sub-item IDs per split.
- Per-split pointers.
- Batch processing of sub-item IDs.
- Candidate retrieval.
- PQTopK scoring.
- Top-K merging.
- Dynamic upper-bound calculation.
- Termination condition.

However, do not mechanically translate TensorFlow operations into C++.

The C++ implementation should use native data structures and algorithms.

The paper's Algorithm 1 is the source of truth for exact algorithmic correctness.

The TensorFlow implementation includes optimisations and configuration options that should be evaluated separately.

## 15. Deliverables

Produce:

1. IndexRecJPQPrune.h
2. IndexRecJPQPrune.cpp
3. RecJPQInvertedLists.h/.cpp, if implemented separately.
4. Unit tests.
5. Benchmark executable or benchmark tests.
6. Faiss build-system integration.
7. Minimal C++ usage example.
8. Documentation describing construction, scoring, search and configuration.

The implementation must compile within the existing Faiss project.

Do not introduce unnecessary external dependencies.

Before finishing:

- Run the Faiss test suite relevant to the new index.
- Run the new unit tests.
- Verify exact equivalence against exhaustive PQTopK.
- Report any deviations from the paper or reference implementation.
- Report benchmark results and memory consumption.

Prioritise a correct, exact CPU implementation. Do not attempt GPU support and advanced SIMD optimisations - these are future work.

import tensorflow as tf
from old_merge import merge_top_k

class PrunedScorer():
    def __init__(self, centroids_per_split, inverted_index, item_codes, item_code_bytes, top_k=10, max_iterations=1000, ub_inflation=1.0, sub_ids_per_iteration = 8):
        self.centroids_per_split = centroids_per_split
        self.item_codes = item_codes
        self.item_code_bytes = item_code_bytes
        self.top_k = top_k
        self.max_iterations = tf.constant(max_iterations, dtype=tf.int32)
        self.ub_inflation = tf.constant(ub_inflation, dtype=tf.float32)
        self.inverted_index = inverted_index
        self.pointers = tf.Variable(tf.zeros(self.item_code_bytes, dtype=tf.int32))
        self.pointer_increments = tf.eye(self.item_code_bytes, dtype=tf.int32) * sub_ids_per_iteration
        self.sub_ids_per_iteration = sub_ids_per_iteration
        self.iteration = tf.Variable(0, dtype=tf.int32)
        self.upper_bound = tf.Variable(float("inf"), dtype=tf.float32)
        self.bound_tensor = tf.constant(tf.fill([self.item_code_bytes, 1], float("-inf")))
        self.num_scored_items = tf.Variable(0, dtype=tf.int32)
        self.last_lower_bound_update = tf.Variable(0, dtype=tf.int32)
        self.threshold = tf.Variable(float("-inf"), dtype=tf.float32)
        self.old_lower_bound = tf.Variable(float("-inf"), dtype=tf.float32)
        self.best_items = tf.Variable(tf.zeros(self.top_k, dtype=tf.int32))
        self.best_values = tf.Variable(tf.zeros(self.top_k, dtype=tf.float32))
        self.scores_with_lower_bound = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([self.item_code_bytes, self.centroids_per_split + 1], dtype=tf.float32))
        self.centroid_scores = tf.Variable(tf.zeros(self.item_code_bytes* self.centroids_per_split, dtype=tf.float32))
        self.items_per_sub_id = inverted_index.shape[1]
        self.sorted_scores_indices = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([self.item_code_bytes, self.centroids_per_split], dtype=tf.int32))

    @tf.function
    def score_top_k(self, items, top_k):
        item_codes = tf.gather(self.item_codes, tf.nn.relu(items)) #we'll filter negative (padding) items later
        mask = tf.cast(items >= 0, tf.float32)
        item_score_full = tf.reduce_sum(tf.gather(self.centroid_scores, item_codes), axis=[1]) * mask + (1-mask)*(-1e9)
        top_k = tf.math.top_k(item_score_full, top_k)
        top_k_items = tf.cast(tf.gather(items, top_k.indices), dtype=tf.int32)
        return top_k_items, top_k.values

    @tf.function
    def __call__(self, centroid_scores):
        self.centroid_scores.assign(centroid_scores)
        centroid_scores_reshaped = tf.reshape(centroid_scores, [self.item_code_bytes, self.centroids_per_split])
        sorted_scores = tf.math.top_k(centroid_scores_reshaped, self.centroids_per_split)
        self.sorted_scores_indices.assign(sorted_scores.indices)
        self.pointers.assign(tf.zeros(self.item_code_bytes, dtype=tf.int32))
        self.upper_bound.assign(float("inf"))
        self.threshold.assign(float("-inf"))
        self.iteration.assign(0)
        self.num_scored_items.assign(0)
        self.last_lower_bound_update.assign(0)
        self.scores_with_lower_bound.assign(tf.concat([sorted_scores.values, self.bound_tensor], axis=1))
        top_scores = tf.gather(self.scores_with_lower_bound, self.pointers, batch_dims=1)
        need_items = self.top_k
        while (tf.sigmoid(self.upper_bound)  > tf.sigmoid(self.threshold) * self.ub_inflation) and (self.iteration < self.max_iterations):
            top_scored_centroid_split_num = tf.argmax(top_scores, output_type=tf.int32)
            top_scored_centroid_num = self.pointers[top_scored_centroid_split_num]
            self.pointers.assign_add(self.pointer_increments[top_scored_centroid_split_num])
            top_scored_centroids = self.sorted_scores_indices[top_scored_centroid_split_num][top_scored_centroid_num:top_scored_centroid_num+self.sub_ids_per_iteration] + top_scored_centroid_split_num * self.centroids_per_split
            items_with_centroids = tf.reshape(tf.gather(self.inverted_index, top_scored_centroids), (self.items_per_sub_id * self.sub_ids_per_iteration,))
            if(self.iteration == 0):
                items, vals = self.score_top_k(items_with_centroids, need_items)
                self.best_items.assign(items)
                self.best_values.assign(vals)
            else:
                items, vals = self.score_top_k(items_with_centroids, need_items)
                merge_top_k(self.best_items, self.best_values, items, vals, self.top_k, need_items)
            self.old_lower_bound.assign(self.threshold)
            self.threshold.assign(self.best_values[-1])
            self.num_scored_items.assign_add(len(items_with_centroids))
            self.iteration.assign_add(1)
            top_scores = tf.gather(self.scores_with_lower_bound, self.pointers, batch_dims=1)
            self.upper_bound.assign(tf.reduce_sum(top_scores))
            n_safe_items = tf.reduce_sum(tf.cast(self.best_values > self.upper_bound, tf.int32))
            need_items = self.top_k - n_safe_items
            if self.old_lower_bound != self.threshold:
                self.last_lower_bound_update.assign(self.iteration)
        return self.best_items, self.best_values

595: # =============================================================================
596: # Dynamic Dispatch Mode
597: # When FAISS_OPT_LEVEL=dd, the main faiss library is built with runtime SIMD
598: # dispatch enabled. This adds FAISS_ENABLE_DD and architecture-specific SIMD
599: # compile definitions to the main faiss target.
600: # =============================================================================
601: if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
602:   # Add SIMD source files to main faiss target for DD builds
603:   target_sources(faiss PRIVATE ${FAISS_SIMD_SRC})
604:   target_compile_definitions(faiss PRIVATE FAISS_ENABLE_DD)
605:   # Architecture-specific SIMD definitions for Dynamic Dispatch
606:   if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(x86_64|amd64|AMD64)")
607:     target_compile_definitions(faiss PRIVATE
608:       COMPILE_SIMD_AVX2
609:       COMPILE_SIMD_AVX512
610:       COMPILE_SIMD_AVX512_VPOPCNT
611:       COMPILE_SIMD_AVX512_SPR)
612:     if(NOT WIN32)
613:       # Baseline flags for common files (prevents auto-vectorization)
614:       target_compile_options(faiss PRIVATE
615:         $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mpopcnt -msse4 -mno-avx -mno-avx2>)
616:       # Per-file SIMD flags (GCC/Clang)
617:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX2_SRC}
618:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
619:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "-mavx2;-mfma;-mf16c;-mpopcnt;-mbmi2"
620:       )
621:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_SRC}
622:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
623:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS
624:           "-mavx512f;-mavx512cd;-mavx512vl;-mavx512dq;-mavx512bw;-mfma;-mf16c;-mpopcnt;-mbmi2"
625:       )
626:       # VPOPCNT sources require VPOPCNTDQ and BITALG on top of baseline AVX-512.
627:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_VPOPCNT_SRC}
628:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
629:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS
630:           "-mavx2;-mfma;-mf16c;-mavx512f;-mavx512cd;-mavx512vl;-mavx512dq;-mavx512bw;-mavx512vpopcntdq;-mavx512bitalg;-mpopcnt;-mbmi2"
631:       )
632:       # The remaining SPR sources require the full SPR feature set.
633:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_SPR_SRC}
634:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
635:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS
636:           "-mavx2;-mfma;-mf16c;-mavx512f;-mavx512cd;-mavx512vl;-mavx512dq;-mavx512bw;-mavx512vpopcntdq;-mavx512bitalg;-mpopcnt;-mavx512vnni;-mavx512fp16;-mavx512bf16;-mbmi2"
637:       )
638:     else()
639:       # Per-file SIMD flags (MSVC)
640:       add_compile_options(/bigobj)
641:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX2_SRC}
642:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
643:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "/arch:AVX2"
644:       )
645:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_SRC}
646:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
647:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "/arch:AVX512"
648:       )
649:       # MSVC has no per-feature flag for VPOPCNTDQ or BITALG.
650:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_VPOPCNT_SRC}
651:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
652:         PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "/arch:AVX512"
653:       )
654:       set_source_files_properties(${FAISS_SIMD_AVX512_SPR_SRC}
655:         TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss

657:       )

678: # NEON is mandatory on ARM64 — ensure COMPILE_SIMD_ARM_NEON is always defined
679: # and NEON source files are always compiled into the main faiss target.
680: # (On x86, AVX2/AVX512 are optional and only compiled per opt_level above.)
681: # MSVC on Windows ARM64 is excluded: simdlib_neon.h takes the address of NEON
682: # intrinsics as non-type template parameters, but MSVC implements many of them
683: # as macros/compiler builtins, so &vmulq_u16 et al. are not usable. MSVC ARM64
684: # falls back to simdlib_emulated.h, matching the pre-D95392150 behavior.
685: if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(aarch64|arm64|ARM64)" AND NOT MSVC)
686:   target_compile_definitions(faiss PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_ARM_NEON)
687:   target_sources(faiss PRIVATE ${FAISS_SIMD_NEON_SRC})
688:   # GCC requires +fp16 for the vector conversion intrinsics in this source.
689:   set_source_files_properties(utils/simd_impl/fp16_kernels_neon.cpp
690:     TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
691:     PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "-march=armv8.2-a+fp16"
692:   )
693: endif()

695: # RVV is the baseline SIMD on rv64 builds; the RVV translation units require
696: # rv64gcv + Zvfhmin (see the RISCV_RVV contract in utils/simd_levels.h), so
697: # they are compiled with -march=rv64gcv_zvfhmin. Compile RVV
698: # sources into the main faiss target, mirroring the ARM NEON story on aarch64.
699: # Guard against DD mode: in dd builds, FAISS_SIMD_SRC already contains
700: # FAISS_SIMD_RVV_SRC and is added via target_sources above, so we must not
701: # add it a second time or we get duplicate symbol errors at link time.
702: if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(riscv64|riscv)" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
703:   target_compile_definitions(faiss PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_RISCV_RVV)

707:       TARGET_DIRECTORY faiss
708:       PROPERTIES COMPILE_OPTIONS "-march=rv64gcv_zvfhmin;-mabi=lp64d"
709:     )

> Abstract:A large item catalogue is a major challenge for deploying modern sequential recommender models, since it makes the memory footprint of the model large and increases inference latency. One promising approach to address this is RecJPQ, which replaces item embeddings with sub-item embeddings. However, slow inference remains problematic because finding the top highest-scored items usually requires scoring all items in the catalogue, which may not be feasible for large catalogues. By adapting dynamic pruning concepts from document retrieval, we propose the RecJPQPrune dynamic pruning algorithm to efficiently find the top highest-scored items without computing the scores of all items in the catalogue. Our RecJPQPrune algorithm is safe-up-to-rank K since it theoretically guarantees that no potentially high-scored item is excluded from the final top K recommendation list, thereby ensuring no impact on effectiveness. Our experiments on two large datasets and three recommendation models demonstrate the efficiency achievable using RecJPQPrune: for instance, on the Tmall dataset with 2\.2M items, we can reduce the median model scoring time by 64 times compared to the Transformer Default baseline, and 5\.3 times compared to a recent scoring approach called PQTopK. Overall, this paper demonstrates the effective and efficient inference of Transformer-based recommendation models at catalogue scales not previously reported in the literature. Indeed, our RecJPQPrune algorithm can score 2 million items in under 10 milliseconds without GPUs, and without relying on Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) techniques.

## 1\. Introduction

Sequential recommender systems use lists of user-item interactions to predict the next item a user is likely to interact with. Using the ordering of interactions allows a recommender system to account for evolving user interests as well as sequential patterns in item interactions common in real-world applications, e.g., users prefer to watch a movie series from the first to the last. The *next item prediction* task tackled by sequential recommender systems is similar to the next token prediction task addressed by language models. Therefore, models that were initially developed for language modelling have been successfully adapted for sequential recommendation. In particular, Transformer-based models ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#bib.bib49)), such as models based on BERT4Rec ([Sun et al., 2019](#bib.bib43); [Du et al., 0 17](#bib.bib15)) and SASRec ([Kang and McAuley, 2018](#bib.bib21); [Petrov and Macdonald, 2023b](#bib.bib34)) have achieved state-of-the-art results for the next item prediction task. To solve the next item prediction task, these models use item ids in place of token ids.

However, despite similarities with language modelling, the number of items in the catalogue of a typical industrial recommender system may be several orders of magnitude larger compared with the vocabulary size of a typical language model ([Zivic et al., 2024](#bib.bib57); [Zhai et al., 2024](#bib.bib54)). In particular, Transformer-based language models, such as BERT ([Devlin et al., 2019](#bib.bib13)), typically have vocabularies of less than 50,000 tokens. In contrast, the number of items in the catalogues of recommender systems can reach hundreds of millions of items on large-scale platforms, such as Amazon or YouTube ([you, 2023](#bib.bib3); [Ama, 2023](#bib.bib2)). A large catalogue results in problems such as large GPU memory requirements for storing item embeddings, slow training and slow model inference ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2024](#bib.bib36); [Petrov and Macdonald, 2022](#bib.bib32)).

This paper specifically focuses on the *slow inference problem*: a typical recommender system works using the "score-and-rank" approach, where the model first scores *all* items in the catalogue and then selects the top KK items according to their scores. In contrast, in this paper, we consider a scenario in which scoring all items in the catalogue is impractical due to the large catalogue size. Existing methods for avoiding exhaustive scoring rely on heuristics, such as Approximate Nearest Neighbours (ANN) ([Chen et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)). However, these heuristics are *unsafe*, meaning that they do not provide theoretical guarantees that all highly-scored items are included in the recommendation list, and hence can result in degraded effectiveness. Moreover, most ANN-based methods require full item embeddings to be trained in the first place, which may not be feasible in the large catalogue scenario ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2024](#bib.bib36)). Therefore, our goal is to develop a *safe* method that guarantees no degradation in recommendation effectiveness by finding the exact top KK highest-scoring items while only scoring *some* items in the catalogue. To achieve this, we build upon salient characteristics of RecJPQ ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2024](#bib.bib36)) – a recently proposed embedding compression method for recommender systems.

RecJPQ splits item ids into a limited number of shared *sub-item ids*, akin to how language models split words into shared subword tokens. Item embeddings can then be constructed as a concatenation of the sub-item embeddings, which results in substantially smaller models compared to storing full item embeddings. While helping to compress the model, the method does not fully solve the slow inference problem. Indeed, even the PQTopK ([Petrov et al., 2024](#bib.bib37)) algorithm (the most optimised version of the RecJPQ-based inference algorithm to date) still applies the score-and-rank approach, which requires scoring all items. However, we observe that the way PQTopK computes item scores given the scores of its sub-items is similar to how traditional information retrieval (IR) models compute document scores given a query: an item score can be computed as the sum of the scores of the individual sub-items, which is similar to computing document score as a sum of token scores in the "bag-of-word" retrieval method, such as BM25 ([Robertson et al., 1994](#bib.bib41)).

This inspires us to examine the applicability of dynamic pruning techniques that are typically employed to increase the efficiency of bag-of-word retrieval methods. Indeed, in this work, we propose the pruning-based RecJPQPrune method for efficient calculation of top KK ranked items under RecJPQ. The idea of this novel method is based on the hypothesis that highly-ranked items should also have highly-scored sub-items. Instead of exhaustively computing scores for all items in the catalogue, we only compute scores for items that are associated with the highest-scored sub-items. Moreover, the specifics of sub-item representations in RecJPQ allow us to compute an upper bound for the item scores, which allows us to stop the item scoring way before all items in the catalogue have been scored.

Recent generative recommender systems, such as TIGER ([Rajput et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)) and GPTRec ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2023a](#bib.bib33)), also rely on sub-item representations and avoid exhaustive item scoring by generating item ids autoregressively. However, both TIGER and GPTRec mention generation speed as a limitation, as they require a Transformer invocation for every generated sub-id, which makes them inefficient for retrieval and outside the scope of this paper.

In summary, this work contributes: (1) a novel dynamic pruning approach, RecJPQPrune, for speeding up inference for large-catalogue RecJPQ-based recommender models, with no impact on effectiveness; (2) experiments examining median and tail scoring times on two large datasets with millions of items, and for three Transformer-based sequential recommender models; and (3) a study into factors affecting the efficiency of RecJPQPrune for different models and different users. RecJPQPrune provides marked efficiency benefits – for instance, on the Tmall dataset with 2\.2M items, we can reduce the median model scoring time by 64×\\times compared to default Transformer scoring, and 5\.3×\\times compared to PQTopK.

## 2\. Pruning in Document Retrieval

In the classical document retrieval task, the goal of the IR system is to retrieve textual *documents* from a document collection 𝒟\\mathcal{D} that are estimated most likely to be *relevant* to a given textual query qq. We focus on "bag-of-word" retrieval approaches, as exemplified by BM25 ([Robertson et al., 1994](#bib.bib41)), in which both the documents d∈𝒟d\\in\\mathcal{D} and the query qq are represented as multisets of *terms* tt. Bag-of-word approaches compute query-document relevance estimates as:

(1) |  | score​(q,d)=∑t∈qw⁡(t,d)\\displaystyle\\text{score}(q,d)=\\sum\_{t\\in q}w(t,d) |

Each document has a non-negative integer known as a document identifier (docid). Every term present in the collection has a posting list, which comprises the docids of all documents where the term appears. The aggregated posting lists for all terms form the inverted index of 𝒟\\mathcal{D}. The docids within a posting list can be arranged in ascending order, or by descending score/impact ([Anh et al., 2001](#bib.bib4)). The traditional approaches for processing queries and matching them to documents are the term-at-a-time (TAAT) strategy, where the posting lists of query terms are processed sequentially, and the scores for each document are summed up in an accumulator data structure; or document-at-a-time (DAAT), where the posting lists of query terms are processed simultaneously while maintaining docid alignment.

Processing queries exhaustively with TAAT or DAAT can be very inefficient. As a result, various dynamic pruning techniques ([Tonellotto et al., 2018](#bib.bib47)) have been proposed,11 1 In the deep learning literature, the term *pruning* typically means *weight pruning*. In our case, we use the term pruning as used in IR literature ([Tonellotto et al., 2018](#bib.bib47)) meaning pruning candidates from the scoring process to speed up scoring. For applications of weight pruning to recommender systems see, for example, ([Shen et al., 2021](#bib.bib42)) or ([Deng et al., 2021](#bib.bib12))., which aim to omit the scoring of (portions of) documents during query processing if they cannot make the final top KK retrieved set. Dynamic pruning strategies can be described as safe-up-to-rank KK – meaning they are guaranteed to calculate the exact scores for each retrieved document, at least as deep as rank KK – or unsafe – indicating that their retrieval effectiveness may be negatively impact compared to an exhaustive scoring.

All dynamic pruning optimisations for TAAT involve a two-phase strategy. In the initial phase, the TAAT algorithm is applied, processing one term at a time in ascending order of document frequency. New accumulators are created and updated until a pruning condition is satisfied. Subsequently, the second phase commences, during which no new accumulators are created ([Buckley and Lewit, 1985](#bib.bib6); [Moffat and Zobel, 1994](#bib.bib30); [Moffat and Zobel, 1996](#bib.bib31)).

Among the dynamic pruning strategies for DAAT, MaxScore ([Turtle and Flood, 1995](#bib.bib48)), WAND ([Broder et al., 2003](#bib.bib5)), and their variants ([Ding and Suel, 2011](#bib.bib14); [Mallia et al., 2017](#bib.bib29)) stand out as the most widely used. Both approaches enhance the inverted index by recording the maximum score contribution for each term. This enables the safe skipping of substantial segments within posting lists if those segments only consist of terms whose combined maximum scores are lower than the scores of the top KK documents already identified during query processing, known as the threshold, and denoted θ\\theta. They also utilise a global per-term upper bound, i.e., the maximum score across all documents containing the term, in order to make pruning decisions. Finally, there are a number of dynamic pruning strategies for impact-ordered posting lists, such as score-at-a-time ([Anh et al., 2001](#bib.bib4)). Similarly, our approach uses score-sorted ids to perform computations as efficiently as possible ([Mackenzie et al., 2023](#bib.bib28)), but we do not leverage related dynamic pruning techniques e.g. anytime ranking ([Zilberstein, 1996](#bib.bib56)), due to their inherent unsafeness, leaving to future work the analysis of unsafe settings.

In this paper, we propose a safe-up-to-rank-KK novel dynamic pruning strategy, RecJPQPrune, which is a hybrid of both TAAT and DAAT dynamic pruning, but designed specifically for scoring RecJPQ item representations in recommender systems. We position RecJPQPrune within the dynamic pruning literature in Section [4](#S4 "4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings").

Other works focussed on improving the efficiency of expensive machine-learned ranking models have addressed (i) early termination of regression trees ([Cambazoglu et al., 2010](#bib.bib8)), or, (ii) more recently, the early termination of layers in Transformer-based models ([Xin et al., 2020](#bib.bib52)), such as cross-encoders. These optimisations are applied for each candidate document being ranked. In our setting, the Transformer model needs to be applied only once to obtain a representation of the user’s recommendation need, like a query encoder in neural dense document retrieval. Hence, approaches that speed up model inference are orthogonal to our proposed RecJPQPrune strategy.

## 3\. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation

In this section, we cover the background of the large-scale sequential recommendation. Section [3\.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1. Preliminaries ‣ 3. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings") provides an overview of current state-of-the-art models for large-scale sequential recommendation. Section [3\.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2. RecJPQ and PQTopK ‣ 3. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings") details RecJPQ, the state-of-the-art method for item embedding compression and PQTopK, an efficient scoring algorithm for RecJPQ-based models as a baseline for our work.

### 3\.1. Preliminaries

Sequential recommendation is seen as a *next item prediction* task. Formally, given a chronologically ordered sequence of user-item interactions h={i1,i2,i3​…​in}h=\\left\\{i\_{1},i\_{2},i\_{3}...i\_{n}\\right\\}, also known as their interactions history, the goal of a recommender system is to predict the next item in the sequence, in\+1i\_{n+1} from the *item catalogue* ℐ\\mathcal{I}, that is, the set of all possible items. The total number of items \|ℐ\|\|\\mathcal{I}\| is the *catalogue size*.

Sequential recommendation bears a resemblance to the natural language processing task of *next token prediction*, as addressed by language models, such as GPT-2 ([Radford et al., 2019](#bib.bib39)). Hence, language models have been adapted to recommendation, by replacing token ids (in language models) with item ids (in recommendation models). In particular, Transformer-based models ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#bib.bib49)), such as SASRec ([Kang and McAuley, 2018](#bib.bib21)) (based on the Transformer Decoder architecture, like GPT-2) and BERT4Rec ([Sun et al., 2019](#bib.bib43)) (based on Transformer Encoder, like BERT) have exhibited state-of-the-art results for sequential recommendation ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2022](#bib.bib32)).

Typically, to generate recommendations given a history of interactions hh, Transformer-based models first generate a sequence embedding ϕ∈ℝd\\phi\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}, where dd is the embedding dimensionality, using the Transformer model, such that ϕ=Transformer​(h)\\phi=\\textsf{Transformer}(h)22 2 In document retrieval parlance, this would be a query embedding.. The scores for all items, denoted as r=(r1,…,r\|ℐ\|)∈ℝ\|ℐ\|r=(r\_{1},\\ldots,r\_{\|\\mathcal{I}\|})\\in\\mathbb{R}^{\|\\mathcal{I}\|}, are then computed by multiplying the matrix of item embeddings W∈ℝ\|ℐ\|×dW\\in\\mathbb{R}^{\|\\mathcal{I}\|\\times d}, where dd is the embeddings dimension, shared with the embeddings layer of the Transformer model, by the sequence embedding ϕ\\phi:33 3 This generalises to models with item biases (e.g. BERT4Rec) if we assume that the first dimension of the sequence embedding is 1 and the first dimension of item embedding is the bias.

(2) |  | r=W​ϕ\\displaystyle r=W\\phi |

Finally, the model generates recommendations by selecting from rr the top KK items with the highest scores. In the rest of the paper, we refer to this simple matrix-to-vector multiplication-based scoring procedure as *Transformer Default*.

Despite their effectiveness, training Transformer-based models with large item catalogues is a challenging task, as these models typically have to be trained for long time ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2022](#bib.bib32)) and require appropriate selection of training objective ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2023c](#bib.bib35)), negative sampling strategy and loss function ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2023b](#bib.bib34); [Klenitskiy and Vasilev, 2023](#bib.bib22)). Transformer-based models with large catalogues also require a lot of memory to store the item embeddings WW. This problem has recently been addressed by RecJPQ, which we detail in the next section. Finally, another problem of Transformer-based models with large catalogues is their slow inference with large catalogues. Indeed, computing all item scores using Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.1. Preliminaries ‣ 3. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")) may be prohibitively expensive when the item catalogue is large: it requires \|I\|×d\|I\|\\times d scalar multiplications and additions, and, as we noted in Section [1](#S1 "1. Introduction ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"), in real-world recommender systems, the catalogue size \|I\|\|I\| may reach hundreds of millions of items, making exhaustive computation using Equation ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.1. Preliminaries ‣ 3. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")) impractical. Moreover, typically large-catalogue recommender systems have a large number of users as well; therefore, the model has to be used for inference very frequently and, ideally, using only low-cost hardware, i.e., without GPU acceleration. Therefore, real-life recommender systems rarely exhaustively score all items for all users and instead apply unsafe heuristics (i.e. which do not provide theoretical guarantees that all high-scored items will be returned), such as two-stage ranking. However, as we show in Section [4](#S4 "4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"), it is possible to return the top KK items exactly without scoring all items exhaustively for RecJPQ\-based recommendation models. We now discuss the RecJPQ approach itself and how it can be used for efficient model inference.

### 3\.2. RecJPQ and PQTopK

Product Quantisation (PQ) ([Jégou et al., 2011](#bib.bib17)) is a family of methods for compressing embeddings tensors, where the full embeddings are decomposed into sub-embeddings. PQ is an active area of research (e.g. ([Lee and Choi, 2024](#bib.bib23))) and it is widely used in approximate nearest neighbour approaches, exemplified by the FAISS library ([Johnson et al., 2021](#bib.bib20)). PQ requires that the full embeddings already exist; in contrast, RecJPQ ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2024](#bib.bib36)) is a solution for jointly training effective and compressed item embedding tensors in sequential recommender systems instead of training full embeddings and followed by embedding compression (as done by e.g. EODRec ([Xia et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)), LightRec ([Lian et al., 2020](#bib.bib24)) & MDQE ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib50))). While RecJPQ is named after Joint Product Quantisation ([Zhan et al., 2021](#bib.bib55)) (a dense retrieval technique), the main idea of RecJPQ is inspired by tokenisation in language models. Similar to how words are split into sub-word tokens in language models, item ids are split into sub-item ids in RecJPQ. RecJPQ can be used with many embedding-based sequential recommendation models (including state-of-the-art Transformer-based models, such as BERT4Rec). In this section, we provide an overview of RecJPQ and the RecJPQ-based PQTopK approach for efficient scoring ([Petrov et al., 2024](#bib.bib37)).

## 4\. RecJPQPrune

We now describe our RecJPQPrune method, discussing the principles we use for dynamic pruning of RecJPQ-based representations (Section [4\.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Dynamic Pruning Principles for RecJPQPrune ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")), the algorithm itself (Section [4\.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. RecJPQPrune Algorithm ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")), and its positioning w.r.t. existing IR dynamic pruning strategies (Section [4\.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3. Relation to Dynamic Pruning Literature ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")).

### 4\.1. Dynamic Pruning Principles for RecJPQPrune

Our goal is to build an algorithm that allows us to find the top-ranked items while avoiding exhaustive catalogue scoring. In Section [2](#S2 "2. Pruning in Document Retrieval ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"), we discussed that for document retrieval, a similar problem can be solved using pruning techniques. Comparing how document scores are computed in bag-of-word document retrieval models (Equation ([1](#S2.E1 "In 2. Pruning in Document Retrieval ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"))) and how item scores are computed in PQTopK (Equation ([5](#S3.E5 "In 3.2. RecJPQ and PQTopK ‣ 3. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"))), we find parallels between the two: in both cases, the final entity score is computed a sum of individual sub-entity scores. However, addressing the efficient computation of item scores requires the construction of a novel dynamic pruning algorithm. RecJPQPrune is based on three principles that allow the scoring of some items to be omitted. We now describe these principles, while, later in Section [4\.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3. Relation to Dynamic Pruning Literature ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"), we compare and contrast RecJPQPrune with existing dynamic pruning approaches.

#### P1. Items with high scores typically have sub-items with high scores as well

The intuition behind this principle is that the total score of an item is calculated as the sum of its sub-item scores. Hence, a high overall score generally requires several high-scoring sub-items. Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.1. Dynamic Pruning Principles for RecJPQPrune ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings") shows empirical evidence for this principle. The figure illustrates how sub-item id scores are distributed for user 82,082 in the Gowalla dataset computed by the SASRecJPQ model ([Petrov and Macdonald, 2024](#bib.bib36)), where the number of splits M=8M=8 and the number of sub-items per split B=256B=256. In the figure, the sub-item ids are ranked within their splits according to their score, with the highest-scored sub-item ids (bright-yellow colours) being on the left of the figure and the lowest-scored sub-item ids (dark-red colours) being on the right of the figure. The figure highlights the sub-item ids associated with a top-ranked item, a middle-ranked item and a bottom-ranked item. As we can see, all sub-item ids of the top-ranked item appear to the left of the figure, i.e., they are scored high within their respective splits, and have bright colours, i.e., they are scored high across all sub-item ids. For the middle-scored item, we have a mixture of relatively high and relatively low-scored sub-item ids; however, none of the sub-item ids is the highest-scored sub-item id in the respective split. Most of the sub-item ids of the low-scored item also scored low. Overall, Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.1. Dynamic Pruning Principles for RecJPQPrune ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings") supports Principle P1.

In summary, Principle P1 suggests processing first the items associated with highly-scored sub-item ids during scoring before processing those linked to less highly-scored sub-item ids. This ensures we are likely to encounter all high-scored items relatively quickly. However, to achieve efficiency gains compared to exhaustive scoring, we need to be able to terminate scoring after all high-scored items have been found; to do that, we use Principle P2.

#### P2. We can terminate scoring once the remaining items have no chance to enter the top KK results

The unscored, ℐU\\mathcal{I}^{U}, are guaranteed to have all their sub-item ids appearing in UU, because items associated with already processed sub-item ids were scored when their respective sub-item ids were processed. Transformers for Large-catalogue Sequential Recommendation ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings")), we can derive a score upper bound σ\\sigma for any unscored item i∈IUi\\in I^{U}:

some items can still be entered into the top KK items. However, θ\\theta rises as items are admitted into the top KK, and σ\\sigma falls as the unprocessed sub-item ids are less important. In summary, Principle P2 argues that top KK items can be found without exhaustive scoring of all items in the catalogue, and provides us with the pruning condition that helps to identify the moment when scoring can be terminated.

#### P3. Highly scored sub-item ids are frequently found in the same split.

In RecJPQ, sub-item ids are obtained using SVD decomposition of the user-item interaction matrix with different splits corresponding to different latent features of items. This means that if two items had similar values of a latent feature in the SVD decomposition, they would also have similar sub-item ids in the corresponding split. In short, in RecJPQ, *similar items are assigned to similar sub-item ids*. As a result, in RecJPQ, highly scored sub-item ids are frequently clustered in the same split. For example, looking again at Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.1. Dynamic Pruning Principles for RecJPQPrune ‣ 4. RecJPQPrune ‣ Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of Sub-Item Embeddings"), we see that most of the highly-scored sub-item ids for the illustrated user are located in the last split. This suggests that once we find a promising sub-item id, we can process not only items associated with this sub-item id, but also items associated with other highly-scored sub-item ids from the same split. In other words, Principle P3 allows for *batch processing* of sub-item ids.

#define READ1(x) READANDCHECK(&(x), 1)

// Reads a single byte into a bool, rejecting any byte that is not the
// canonical encoding for the platform's bool representation. Reading a
// non-canonical byte directly into a bool is undefined behavior and
// trips UBSan's invalid-bool-load check. To stay ABI-portable, we
// assign via the language-defined conversion (b != 0) and then compare
// the resulting bool's storage byte back against the byte we read - the
// roundtrip succeeds iff the input byte was already canonical on this
// platform. FAISS only ever writes the canonical encoding via
// WRITE1(bool), so well-formed indices roundtrip cleanly; corrupt or
// attacker-controlled input that places a non-canonical byte at a bool
// offset is rejected as a FaissException.
#define READ1_BOOL(x)                                                      \
    {                                                                      \
        static_assert(                                                     \
                sizeof(x) == 1, "READ1_BOOL: destination must be 1 byte"); \
        uint8_t b;                                                         \
        READANDCHECK(&b, 1);                                               \
        (x) = (b != 0);                                                    \
        FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT_FMT(                                            \
                *reinterpret_cast<const uint8_t*>(&(x)) == b,              \
                "invalid bool encoding 0x%02x for %s",                     \
                b,                                                         \
                #x);                                                       \
    }

#define READ1_DUMMY(x_type) \

## Objective
Implement RecJPQPrune (Petrov et al., SIGIR 2025, arXiv:2505.00560) as a native Faiss index `faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune` in /Users/craig.macdonald/git/faiss (Faiss 1.16.0-dev), with CSR inverted lists, exact top-K search via the paper's Algorithm 1, unit tests, benchmarks, build integration, a demo, and documentation. All changes so far are uncommitted.

## Requirements
- Derive `IndexRecJPQPrune` directly from `faiss::Index` (NOT IndexFlatCodes/IndexIVF); METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT only; higher scores better; results descending score; pad missing with -inf/-1.
- Data model: N×M uint8 codes (B ≤ 256, documented), codebooks [M][B][ds] with ds = d/M, arbitrary int64 external IDs, internal positions in [0,N).
- Dedicated CSR inverted lists class `RecJPQInvertedLists` (two-pass build, no padding, no per-list allocations, `build`/`list_size`/`get_list`/`get_list_range`).
- Scoring: precompute S[m][b] = dot(codebooks[m][b], phi_m) once per query; item score = sum_m S[m][codes[i][m]] (PQTopK lookup, no full dot products during search).
- Exact pruning: default exact mode (ub_inflation=1.0, no arbitrary iteration cap, no early termination, sigma ≤ theta condition), handle negatives/empty lists/BS>B; document a deterministic tie policy; report incompleteness if max_iterations hit.
- Dedup via uint32 generation counter (never shared between concurrent searches); thread-safe concurrent `search()`.
- Construction API: `IndexRecJPQPrune(d, M, B)` + `build(n, item_codes, codebooks, ids=nullptr)`; no need for full embeddings; clear ownership (data copied).
- Deliverables: .h/.cpp for index and inverted lists, unit tests, benchmark executable, CMake integration, minimal C++ example, documentation. Before finishing: run Faiss tests + new tests, verify exact equivalence vs exhaustive PQTopK, report deviations + benchmark/memory results.
- No GPU, no advanced SIMD (future work).

## Decisions
- Construction via `build()`; `add()`/`add_with_ids()` throw with informative messages; `add_sa_codes()` supported (append codes, rebuild CSR, O(N) per call); `sa_code_size()=M`, `sa_decode()` implemented.
- Tie policy (documented in header): ties broken by discovery order (first-seen wins); Q[m] sorted by (score desc, sub-item id asc); argmax m* ties → lowest m; makes σ ≤ θ termination exact.
- Top-K merge: per-iteration `std::partial_sort` of union (current topK ∪ new candidates) with unique per-query `seq` counter; theta = k-th score when k items collected else -inf.
- Per-thread scratch via `std::unordered_map<std::thread::id, std::shared_ptr<ThreadState>>` under mutex with bounded cache (max(8, 2×omp threads)); caller keeps shared_ptr for lifetime safety; visited generation counter with overflow wrap (clear + restart at gen 1).
- `S` matrix computed with M `cblas_sgemv` calls (CblasRowMajor, m=B, n=d_split), matching `ProductQuantizer::compute_LUT` pattern.
- `last_search_complete` is `std::atomic<bool>`; stats via caller-owned `RecJPQPruneStats*` in `SearchParametersRecJPQPrune {batch_size=8, max_iterations=-1, ub_inflation=1.0f, exact_mode=true, stats}`.
- IO: fourcc "IRJQ" in write/read; clone: custom branch in `Cloner::clone_Index` rebuilding via `build()` (class non-copyable due to mutex); default constructor for read_index.

# @lint-ignore-every LICENSELINT
# Copyright (c) Meta Platforms, Inc. and affiliates.
#
# This source code is licensed under the MIT license found in the
# LICENSE file in the root directory of this source tree.

function(link_to_faiss_lib target)
  if(NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx2" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512_spr" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "sve" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx2")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX2>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx2)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma -mavx512f -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX512>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx512)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512_spr")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      # Architecture mode to support AVX512 extensions available since Intel (R) Sapphire Rapids.
      # Ref: https://networkbuilders.intel.com/solutionslibrary/intel-avx-512-fp16-instruction-set-for-intel-xeon-processor-based-products-technology-guide
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma -mf16c -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw -mavx512vpopcntdq -mavx512bitalg -mpopcnt -mavx512fp16 -mavx512bf16>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX512>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx512_spr)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "sve")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      if("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=native")
        # Do nothing, expect SVE to be enabled by -march=native
      elseif("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )(-march=armv[0-9]+(\\.[1-9]+)?-[^+ ](\\+[^+$ ]+)*)")
        # Add +sve
        target_compile_options(${target}  PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:DEBUG>>:${CMAKE_MATCH_2}+sve>)
      elseif(NOT "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=armv")
        # No valid -march, so specify -march=armv8-a+sve as the default
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:DEBUG>>:-march=armv8-a+sve>)
      endif()
      if("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=native")
        # Do nothing, expect SVE to be enabled by -march=native
      elseif("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )(-march=armv[0-9]+(\\.[1-9]+)?-[^+ ](\\+[^+$ ]+)*)")
        # Add +sve
        target_compile_options(${target}  PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:RELEASE>>:${CMAKE_MATCH_2}+sve>)
      elseif(NOT "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=armv")
        # No valid -march, so specify -march=armv8-a+sve as the default
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:RELEASE>>:-march=armv8-a+sve>)
      endif()
    else()
      # TODO: support Windows
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_sve)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
    # DD mode: link to main faiss library with DD-specific definitions
    # When FAISS_OPT_LEVEL=dd, the main faiss library is built with DD enabled,
    # so we link to faiss (not a separate faiss_dd).
    # FAISS_ENABLE_DD exposes SIMDConfig class to consuming code (e.g., tests)
    # COMPILE_SIMD_* flags enable DD code paths in headers (architecture-specific)
    # Note: No SIMD compile flags here - DD handles dispatch internally.
    # Special tests (like test_simd_levels.cpp) that use raw intrinsics
    # should get their own SIMD flags via set_source_files_properties.
    #
    # Architecture-specific definitions mirror simd_dispatch.bzl dispatch_config:
    # - x86_64: AVX2 + AVX512 enabled
    # - aarch64: ARM_NEON enabled
    target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE FAISS_ENABLE_DD)
    if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(x86_64|amd64|AMD64)")
      target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_AVX2 COMPILE_SIMD_AVX512)
    elseif(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(aarch64|arm64|ARM64)")
      target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_ARM_NEON)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss)
  endif()
endfunction()

# IndexRecJPQPrune: exact top-K search over RecJPQ embeddings with dynamic pruning

Faiss implementation of the dynamic pruning search algorithm from
**"Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of
Sub-Item Embeddings"** (Petrov, Macdonald, Tonellotto, SIGIR 2025,
[arXiv:2505.00560](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00560)), for catalogues of
items whose embeddings are compressed with RecJPQ (Rec-Joint Product
Quantization).

- Class: `faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune` in `faiss/IndexRecJPQPrune.h`
- Inverted lists: `faiss::RecJPQInvertedLists` in `faiss/invlists/RecJPQInvertedLists.h`
- Tests: `tests/test_recjpq_prune.cpp` (22 tests)
- Benchmark: `benchs/bench_recjpq_prune.cpp`
- Demo: `demos/demo_recjpq_prune.cpp`

## Data model

Each of the `N` items is represented by `M` codes (one per *split*), each a
`uint8_t` in `[0, B)` (hence `B <= 256`). The (approximate) embedding of an
item is the concatenation of its `M` *sub-item embeddings* looked up from the
codebooks:

```
embedding(i) = concat( G[0][code(i,0)], G[1][code(i,1)], ..., G[M-1][code(i,M-1)] )
```

with `G[m]` an `B x d_split` codebook and `d_split = d / M`. Only
`METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT` is supported (higher score is better); results are
returned in descending score order, padded with `(-1, -inf)` when fewer than
`k` items exist.

The index is *built from pre-computed codes and codebooks* (typically from an
existing `IndexPQ`: codes via `pq.compute()`, codebooks via `pq.centroids`)
— it does not accept dense vectors:

```cpp
faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune index(d, M, B);       // METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT by default
index.build(n, item_codes, codebooks, ids);   // ids optional (default 0..n-1)
```

`item_codes` is a row-major `N x M` `uint8_t` matrix (code at split `m` of
item `i` at `item_codes[i*M + m]`); `codebooks` is row-major
`M*B*d_split` floats (`G[m][b][j]` at `codebooks[(m*B + b)*d_split + j]`).
All data is copied (the index owns its storage). `build()` on a non-empty
index throws; use `reset()` first. `add()`/`add_with_ids()` throw
(informative messages); `add_sa_codes()` appends RecJPQ codes (the CSR
lists are rebuilt over the whole catalogue, so repeated calls are `O(N)`
each); `sa_decode()` decodes codes back into approximate embeddings.

## Inverted lists (CSR)

`RecJPQInvertedLists` stores the `M*B` posting lists (list `(m, b)` =
positions of the items whose code at split `m` is `b`) in CSR style:

- `offsets`: `M*B + 1` boundaries;
- `item_ids`: one contiguous array of `N*M` internal positions, in
  ascending item order within each list.

Two-pass construction (count, prefix sum, fill), no per-list allocation, no
padding for empty lists. Accessors: `list_size`, `get_list` (`nullptr` for
empty lists), `get_list_range`, `total_entries`.

The posting storage is the dominant memory cost: `N*M*sizeof(idx_t)` bytes
(e.g. 64 MB for `N = 10^6, M = 8`).

## Scoring

The search uses the PQTopK scoring function: for query `phi`, the
`M x B` sub-item score matrix is computed **once** per query

```
S[m][b] = dot(G[m][b], phi_m)
```

(M `sgemm` calls, `1 x d_split` by `d_split x B`), and each item is scored
by a table lookup `score(i) = sum_m S[m][code(i,m)]` — no full dot product
is computed during the search.

## Search algorithm (Algorithm 1 of the paper)

For one query:

1. Compute `S`, and sort the sub-item ids of each split by descending `S`
   (ties: lower sub-item id first), keeping a per-split cursor.
2. Upper bound: `sigma = sum_m S[m][next unprocessed sub-item of split m]`
   (`-inf` for an exhausted split).
3. Threshold: `theta` = score of the current `k`-th best item (`-inf` until
   `k` items have been scored).
4. While `sigma > theta`:
   - pick the split `m*` whose next unprocessed sub-item scores highest
     (ties: lowest `m` first);
   - process the next `batch_size` sub-item ids of that split (clamped at
     `B`);
   - the union of their posting lists yields new candidate items
     (deduplicated by internal position with a per-thread generation
     counter);
   - score the candidates with the `S` lookup table and merge them into the
     running top-K (`partial_sort` of the union, keeping
     `min(k, |union|)`);
   - update `theta` and `sigma`.

**Correctness / exactness.** Every item not yet scored has an unprocessed
code in every split, so its score is bounded by `sigma`; when `sigma <=
theta`, no unscored item can enter the top-K, and the result is the *exact*
top-K under the tie-breaking policy below. In exact mode (default) the loop
runs until that condition holds — there is no iteration cap and no early
termination. If `max_iterations` (approximate mode only) is reached first,
the result is the best top-K over the items scored so far and
`last_search_complete` is set to `false`.

### Tie-breaking policy (deterministic)

Ties in item score are broken by **discovery order**: the item that first
entered a candidate batch (earlier main-loop iteration, then earlier
position within the batch) ranks first. Implementation: each scored item
carries a per-query unique discovery sequence; the top-K merge orders by
`(score desc, sequence asc)`. Sub-item id ties are broken by ascending sub
item id, and split ties by the lowest split index. With this policy an
unscored item tying `theta` necessarily loses the tie-break against an
already scored one, so `sigma <= theta` remains an exact termination
condition (the paper's correctness argument, made deterministic).

## Configuration

Index-level defaults (all written/read with the index):

| member | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `batch_size` | 8 | sub-item ids processed per main-loop iteration (`BS` in the paper) |
| `max_iterations` | -1 | main-loop iteration cap; -1 = unlimited (ignored in exact mode) |
| `ub_inflation` | 1.0 | threshold multiplier in approximate mode: stop at `sigma <= theta * ub_inflation` |
| `exact_mode` | true | run to exact `sigma <= theta` termination (forces `ub_inflation = 1.0`, ignores `max_iterations`) |

`SearchParametersRecJPQPrune` (passed to `search`) overrides these and can
point at a caller-owned `RecJPQPruneStats`:

```
iterations, items_scored, postings_traversed, sub_items_processed,
final_sigma, final_theta
```

(counters accumulate over the queries of one `search` call).

`last_search_complete` (`std::atomic<bool>`) reports whether the most
recent `search` ran every query to exact termination.

## Thread safety

`search`, `reconstruct*`, `score_item`, `compute_sub_item_scores` and
`sa_decode` are `const` and safe to call concurrently. Per-thread scratch
(score matrix, sorted id lists, top-K, deduplication generation table) is
cached in a bounded per-thread-state map; the deduplication table is a
`uint32` generation counter per item, never shared between searches, and
wraps safely (table cleared, generation restarted). `build`/`add_sa_codes`/
`reset` take exclusive access and must not run concurrently with searches.

## Persistence and cloning

`write_index`/`read_index` support the index with fourcc `"IRJQ"` (layout:
index header, `M`, `B`, search defaults, item codes, ids, codebooks, CSR
offsets and item ids; sizes are validated on read). `clone_index` produces
an independent copy (the class is not copy-assignable because of its
internal mutexes). `reconstruct(key)`, `reconstruct_batch` and
`reconstruct_n(i0, ni)` use external-id semantics (Faiss convention);
`reconstruct_positions(i0, ni)` uses internal positions.

## Differences from the paper / TF reference

- **Termination.** The paper's Algorithm 1 iterates while `sigma > theta`
  exactly as implemented. The TensorFlow reference (`pruned_score_batch.py`)
  compares `sigmoid(sigma) > sigmoid(theta) * ub_inflation`; this is
  algebraically identical at `ub_inflation = 1.0`. Here `ub_inflation` is
  applied directly as `sigma <= theta * ub_inflation` (same effect, no
  sigmoid).
- **Batch scoring.** The TF reference scores only the top of each batch;
  here all new candidates of a batch are scored. Both are exact; scoring
  them all keeps the code simple and is the same asymptotic work, since
  every candidate is scored at most once per query (deduplication).
- **Storage.** The TF reference uses a dense, `-1`-padded inverted index;
  the CSR layout here stores no padding.
- **`B > 256` is not supported** (item codes are `uint8_t`); the paper does
  not impose this limit.

## Building and running

The index is registered in `faiss/CMakeLists.txt` (main library), the test
in `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, and the benchmark/demo are `EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL`
targets:

```
cmake --build build --target faiss_test
./build/tests/faiss_test --gtest_filter='*RecJPQ*'

cmake --build build --target bench_recjpq_prune demo_recjpq_prune
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 ./build/benchs/bench_recjpq_prune [N] [n_queries] [k] [random|structured]
./build/demos/demo_recjpq_prune
```

## Benchmark results

Apple Silicon (M-series), clang 23, `-O3` Release, single OpenBLAS/OpenMP
thread, `M = 8, B = 256, d_split = 64` (d = 512), `N = 10^6`, `k = 100`,
100 unit-norm Gaussian queries. Codes uniform; `random` codebooks i.i.d.
Gaussian (hard case: no score hierarchy); `structured` codebooks = unit
directions scaled by log-normal magnitudes (emulates the wide spread of
sub-item scores in real recommendation embeddings).

Memory: build ~24 ms; index footprint **76.8 MiB** (8 MB codes + 8 MB ids +
0.5 MB codebooks + 64 MB CSR postings).

Exhaustive PQTopK baseline (score all items + top-K selection):
**3.6-3.7 ms/query**.

| dataset | batch | median ms | p95 ms | items scored | % of catalogue | iterations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| random | 1 | 7.06 | 8.02 | 537,807 | 53.8 | 187 |
| random | 8 | 6.96 | 8.21 | 546,009 | 54.6 | 24 |
| random | 64 | 11.30 | 11.94 | 809,006 | 80.9 | 5 |
| structured | 1 | **1.40** | 2.30 | 116,867 | **11.7** | 32 |
| structured | 2 | 1.41 | 2.34 | 121,624 | 12.2 | 16 |
| structured | 8 | 1.86 | 2.67 | 166,047 | 16.6 | 5 |
| structured | 64 | 10.10 | 11.24 | 671,771 | 67.2 | 4 |

On the structured catalogue the pruning scores ~12% of the items and is
~2.6x faster than exhaustive; on purely random data there is no structure
to exploit and the cost is comparable (this is a lower bound on the
overhead of the machinery). Exactness: in both datasets the top-`k` score
vectors match the exhaustive baseline bit-for-bit (max abs diff 0).

`batch_size` trades work against parallelism within a batch: small batches
do the least total work (each sub-item's posting list is deduplicated
against everything seen so far), while large batches traverse more postings
before the threshold drops. `1..4` is the sweet spot in this configuration.

## Limitations / future work

- No GPU support; the inner loop is scalar (SIMD of the `S` lookups and the
  merge are straightforward future work).
- `add_sa_codes` rebuilds the CSR lists in `O(N)`; a true incremental CSR
  append would need a re-merge of the posting arrays.
- The per-query per-thread scratch is allocated on first use (a few hundred
  KB at `B = 256`) and cached for the life of the thread pool.
